## About the Author

::: {.dashboard-card}
- **Author:** **Emma Acedo Lapieza**
- **Project:** Milestone 6 — *Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics? (1896–2016)*
- **GitHub Repository:** [`https://github.com/emmaacedoo/beyond-the-medals`](https://github.com/emmaacedoo/beyond-the-medals)
- **Published Website:** [`https://emmaacedoo.github.io/beyond-the-medals/`](https://emmaacedoo.github.io/beyond-the-medals/)

I created this project because I love sports and wanted to explore 120 years of Olympic history through data science in R and Quarto. Coming from **Spain (`ESP`)**, I was especially curious to see how European nations compare against the United States—both individually and as a combined group—how national GDP relates to Olympic medal counts, and how Spain's Olympic medal performance changed during and after the **1992 Barcelona Olympics**.
:::

---

## Project Overview & Key Findings

::: {.dashboard-card}
Looking at 120 years of Olympic data from **1896 to 2016**, our multi-page exploration reveals five core takeaways:

1. **Individual Athlete Physical Profiles (`14,553` Plotted Observations on the Homepage):**
   - On the [Home page](index.html), we plot **14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations directly** (**4,595** from the United States and **9,958** from the 12 selected European countries) with recorded `Age` and `Height`.
   - Each point represents a single athlete-event observation, showing that U.S. Olympic medalists are on average slightly younger (**24.6 years** vs. **26.6 years**) and taller (**180.0 cm** vs. **178.0 cm**) than their European counterparts.
2. **Group vs. Single-Country Medal Dominance ([USA vs. Europe](usa-vs-europe.html)):**
   - **As a group of 12 countries**, our selected European nations (`ESP`, `GBR`, `FRA`, `GER`, `ITA`, `SWE`, `NOR`, `NED`, `HUN`, `FIN`, `SUI`, `POL`) have won more combined unique event medals (**6,849**) than the United States (**2,823**), because 12 separate nations can enter many more athletes and teams across every event.
   - **As a single country**, the **United States (`2,823` medals)** is by far the most dominant individual nation in Olympic history, winning nearly triple the medals of the highest-ranking European country in our group, **Germany (`1,004`)**, followed by **Great Britain (`919`)** and **France (`879`)**.
3. **Sport Specialization ([Sports](sports.html)):**
   - Even against all 12 European countries combined, the **United States leads in Swimming (`550` vs. `411`)** and is virtually tied in **Athletics (`816` vs. `822`)**, while the 12 European nations hold large collective advantages in **Fencing (`424` vs. `32`)**, **Cycling (`423` vs. `57`)**, **Canoeing (`329` vs. `16`)**, and **Rowing (`314` vs. `89`)**.
4. **Does Money Buy Olympic Success? ([Money & Medals](money-and-medals.html)):**
   - Combining World Bank GDP (`NY.GDP.MKTP.CD`, 1960–2016) with verified Olympic country codes shows a strong positive correlation between log-GDP and log-medals ($r = 0.72$ in Rio 2016), while also demonstrating why GDP is not direct sports funding and why correlation does not prove causation.
5. **Spain's 1992 Barcelona Turning Point ([Barcelona 1992](barcelona-1992.html)):**
   - Through 2016, **Spain (`ESP`)** has won **150 unique event medals** (**45 Gold**, **63 Silver**, and **42 Bronze**), led by **Sailing (`19`)**, **Canoeing (`16`)**, **Cycling (`15`)**, **Athletics (`14`)**, and **Tennis (`12`)**. Spain's Summer Olympic results jumped from an average of **1.6 medals per Games** before 1992 (`26` Summer medals across `16` Games) to **22 Summer medals (`13 Gold`)** at the **1992 Barcelona Summer Olympics**, and remained elevated at **16.7 medals per Games** from `1996` to `2016`.
:::

## Dataset Attribution & Reproducibility

::: {.dashboard-card}
- **Dataset 1 (Olympic Athletes & Results):** [**120 Years of Olympic History: Athletes and Results**](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/heesoo37/120-years-of-olympic-history-athletes-and-results)
  - **Author / Curator:** rgriffin (`heesoo37`) on Kaggle (originally scraped from `www.sports-reference.com` in May 2018)
  - **Scope & Size:** **271,116 rows and 15 columns** covering all Summer and Winter Olympic Games from **Athens 1896 to Rio 2016** (`data/athlete_events.csv` and `data/noc_regions.csv`).
- **Dataset 2 (National GDP):** [**World Bank World Development Indicators — GDP (current US$, `NY.GDP.MKTP.CD`)**](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD)
  - **Scope & Size:** Annual national GDP in current US dollars (`1960–2016`), stored locally in `data/world_bank_gdp.csv` and automatically retrievable via the official World Bank REST API (`https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD`).
- **Key Variables Used:**
  - `ID`, `Name`, `Sex`, `Age`, `Height` (cm), `Weight` (kg)
  - `Team`, `NOC` (3-letter National Olympic Committee code), `iso3c` (ISO-3166 alpha-3 code)
  - `Games`, `Year`, `Season`, `City`
  - `Sport`, `Event`, `Medal` (`Gold`, `Silver`, `Bronze`, or `NA`), `gdp_usd` (World Bank GDP in current US$)

### Reproducibility in This Repository

All three CSV files (`data/athlete_events.csv`, `data/noc_regions.csv`, and `data/world_bank_gdp.csv`) are included directly in the `data/` folder of this repository so that cloning the repository and running `quarto render` reproduces the entire website immediately without external dependencies.

If you ever need to download a fresh copy from Kaggle using the Kaggle CLI:

```bash
mkdir -p data
kaggle datasets download -d heesoo37/120-years-of-olympic-history-athletes-and-results -p data --unzip
```
:::
